de-gesetze.analysis: Round-1 FAIL 1/5 - authoring artifact, not corpus quality. The suite's queries were written with ASCII-transliterated umlauts (Menschenwuerde, muessen, fuer, Moerder) but the norm text has native umlauts, and the analyzer does not fold transliterations: Q2/Q3/Q5 lost their strongest lexical anchors ('Moerder' vs 'Moerder', 'muessen' vs 'muessen'). Q4 (no umlaut anchor needed) passed with the expected file at rank 1. Q1 has no umlauts and missed on BM25 tie-break noise among 3,546 near-uniform tiny norm files (§-250 outranked §-249; a §-37-StVO file entered top-5 on a 'Schaden' stem). FIX pre-registered for round-2: queries re-authored with native umlauts - intent, clauses and expect_files unchanged; this is an encoding correction, not a fit to retrieval output. If Q1 misses again the corpus demotes for real ranking fragility. ROUND 2 RESULT: also FAIL 1/5 - Q4 (the round-1 pass) passed again at rank 1; native umlauts did NOT recover Q2/Q3/Q5 (direct term probes: 'Mörder' matches exactly one file at 9.7, so the analyzer handles umlauts fine; the misses are ranking, not encoding). Mechanism: per-norm files are single-sentence tiny records where inbound §-number references in OTHER sections outweigh the section's own content - the hub-page problem (§-212 Totschlag outranks §-211 Mord for 'Mörder'). Demoted. Round-3 fix pre-registered: re-pin with richer records - per-law files split at § boundaries carrying law name + section heading + full section text, so a record's self-content dominates inbound references.

The #1140 per-file cap cannot help when 10,000 files match.
